content.text: Given that $G$ is the universal gravitational constant, and $g$ is the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity, which statement is true?
The values of $G$ and $g$ depend on location.
The values of $G$ and $g$ are independent of location.
$G$ is the same everywhere in the universe, but $g$ is not.
$g$ is the same everywhere in the universe, but $G$ is not.
One of these two quantities is a property of the universe as a whole; the other is a property of a particular mass at a particular place.
Recall that the field strength at a planet's surface is $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, which depends on the mass $M$ and radius $r$ of the body you are standing on.
C
In the field of a body of mass $M$ and radius $r$ the acceleration due to gravity is given by

so $g$ depends on which body is producing the field and on where you are relative to it. It is not the same on the Earth, on the Moon or on Mars, and it decreases as you move further from the centre. $G$, on the other hand, is a property of the universe: the same value applies between any two masses anywhere in space, which is why it is called the universal gravitational constant.

The true statement is therefore the one saying that $G$ is the same everywhere in the universe but $g$ is not. Option A is wrong because $G$ does not depend on location, and option B is wrong because $g$ plainly does.

items: 1 mark: identifies that $G$ is universal (the same everywhere) while $g$ varies with location, i.e. option C.

content.text: A mass attached to a length of string is moving in a circular path around a central point, O, on a flat, horizontal, frictionless table. This is depicted in the diagram below. The string breaks as the mass passes point X.

content.alt_text: Dashed circular path of the mass about centre O with the string stretched from O to the mass at X. A 'direction of motion' arrow points downwards on the left of the circle. Four candidate paths A, B, C and D radiate from X: A curves back towards the circle, B is straight up (tangential), C curves outwards, and D is straight outwards along the string.

content.text: Which line best depicts the subsequent path of the mass?
Line A
Line B
Line C
Line D
Use the 'direction of motion' arrow on the circle to work out which way the mass is travelling when it passes X on the right-hand side.
Once the string breaks there is no longer a centripetal force, so the mass simply continues with the constant velocity it had at X, along the tangent to its path.
B

The direction-of-motion arrow is drawn on the left of the circle and points downwards, so on the right of the circle, at X, the mass is moving vertically upwards. At X the string OX is horizontal, so the velocity there is perpendicular to the string: it is tangential to the circular path.

The tension in the string is the centripetal force. It is this force that continually turns the velocity vector, keeping the mass on the circle. The instant the string breaks that force disappears, and by Newton's first law the mass continues in a straight line at constant speed in the direction of the velocity it already had.

The path is therefore a straight line along the tangent at X, vertically upwards, which is line B. Line D (straight out along the string) would require the mass to have had no tangential velocity at all; line A (curving back towards the circle) would require a force still pulling it inwards; line C (curving outwards) would require an outward force, which gravity inside the circle can never provide.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the mass continues in a straight line tangent to the circular path at X (line B), because the centripetal force is removed when the string breaks.

content.text: What is the main reason why the Michelson-Morley experiment is considered important?
It shows the existence of the aether.
It suggests that light is an electromagnetic wave.
It indicates that light can exhibit interference effects.
It provides experimental support for the theory of relativity.
Recall what the interferometer actually measured and what result it returned.
A null result rules out the aether hypothesis, so ask which theory a null result is exactly what that theory predicts.
D

Michelson and Morley compared the round-trip travel time of light along two perpendicular arms of an interferometer, one aligned with the Earth's supposed motion through the aether and one at right angles to it. If the aether existed, light would take longer along the arm aligned with the motion, and the interference fringes would shift when the apparatus was rotated through 90 degrees.
No fringe shift was ever detected. The round-trip time was the same in every direction, so the experiment found no evidence at all for the aether.

That null result is exactly what Einstein's special relativity predicts, since the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames. So the experiment is important because it provides experimental support for the theory of relativity. Option A is the opposite of the result, option B is not what an interferometer of this kind demonstrates, and option C confuses the interference used to measure the path difference with a demonstration that light is a wave, which was already well established.

content.text: A stone is thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff and falls onto the beach below. Which acceleration–time graph best describes the motion of the stone?

content.alt_text: Option A: acceleration–time graph with a constant positive value, then a discontinuous step down to a constant negative value, plotted against $t$.
Option B: acceleration–time graph showing a constant positive value for most of the flight, then a vertical drop to zero, plotted against $t$.
Option C: acceleration–time graph showing a curve that rises from the origin to a maximum then falls back to zero, plotted against $t$.
Option D: acceleration–time graph showing a straight line decreasing linearly from a positive value to zero, plotted against $t$.

content.text: Near the Earth's surface gravity is essentially constant, so decide what the acceleration graph looks like from the instant the stone leaves the thrower's hand.
Then consider what happens to the acceleration once the stone has landed and come to rest.
B
Once the stone has left the thrower's hand the only force acting on it is its weight, so its acceleration is constant for the whole flight:

A horizontal launch does not change this. The horizontal velocity stays constant and the vertical velocity increases steadily, but the acceleration is the same in both directions throughout the fall, so the graph is a horizontal line at a constant positive value.

When the stone reaches the beach it stops accelerating, so the graph drops vertically to zero. That is graph B. Graph A is wrong because the acceleration never reverses direction; graphs C and D are wrong because the acceleration does not change gradually during the fall.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the acceleration remains a constant positive value equal to $g$ during the fall and then drops to zero once the stone lands (option B).

Both satellites orbit the same central mass, so Kepler's third law applies with the same constant: $\frac{r^3}{T^2} = \frac{GM}{4\pi^2}$.
Take the ratio for the two satellites so that $G$ and $M$ cancel, then evaluate $\left(\frac{R}{16R}\right)^{3/2}$.
D
Kepler's third law, from Newton's law of universal gravitation applied to a circular orbit, gives
Since both satellites orbit the Earth, the same $G$ and $M$ apply to each. Dividing the two equations eliminates them and leaves the radius ratio:

The satellite in the larger orbit has the longer period, by a factor of 64 rather than 16, because the period depends on the three-halves power of the orbital radius. The satellites' masses do not enter at all.

content.text: The diagram shows a magnet standing on the bottom of a dish filled with a conducting solution. A copper wire is suspended freely from a point above the magnet with its tip in the conducting solution. It is held in the position shown.

content.alt_text: Bar magnet standing in a dish of conducting solution with the N pole at the top and the S pole at the bottom. A copper wire slants from a pivot above the magnet down into the solution with its tip submerged, and a switch and cell are connected to the wire.

content.text: The switch is closed and the wire released. Which of the following will be observed?
The wire will rotate about the magnet.
The wire will be attracted to the magnet.
The magnet will rotate about its vertical axis.
The solution in the dish will rotate about the magnet.
Closing the switch drives a current down the slanting copper wire, and the submerged part of that wire lies in the field between the magnet's poles.
Ask what force acts on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and about which point that force will turn the suspended wire.
A

When the switch is closed a current flows down the copper wire, and the lower part of the wire sits in the magnetic field of the bar magnet, which points from the N pole to the S pole across the dish. A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, the motor effect, of magnitude $F = BIL\sin\theta$.

The wire is pivoted at the point above the magnet, so the magnetic force on the current-carrying part has a moment about that pivot. The free end of the wire therefore swings around the magnet. The wire is not attracted to the magnet as a whole, because the magnet's field and the forces on the two sides of the current do not combine to pull the wire inwards, and neither the magnet nor the conducting solution is free to rotate about a vertical axis.
The wire turning about the magnet is response A.

items: 1 mark: recognises the motor effect — current in the copper wire in the magnet's field produces a force that turns the wire about the magnet (option A).

content.alt_text: Dotted vertical rotation axis passing through a uniform magnetic field drawn as a grid of dots, with a small loop of wire drawn around the axis and an arrow showing the sense of rotation, labelled Axis.

content.text: Which graph best represents the variation of the magnetic flux through the loop with time?

content.alt_text: Option A: magnetic flux starts at a maximum positive value, falls smoothly to a negative minimum and returns to the starting value, plotted against $t$.
Option B: magnetic flux starts at zero, rises smoothly to a positive maximum, falls through zero to a negative minimum and returns to zero, plotted against $t$.
Option C: magnetic flux shows four identical positive humps, each returning to zero, plotted against $t$.
Option D: magnetic flux is a square wave switching between a constant positive and a constant negative value, plotted against $t$.

content.text: Write the flux as $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ and track $\theta$, the angle between $B$ and the normal to the loop, at $t = 0$ and a quarter of a turn later.
A quantity that starts at its extreme value and then varies smoothly looks different on a graph from one that starts at zero.
A

The flux through a loop is $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the field and the normal to the plane of the loop. At $t = 0$ the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field, so the normal is parallel to it, $\theta = 0^{\circ}$, and the flux is at its maximum:

The loop turns at constant rate, so $\theta$ increases steadily and the flux falls smoothly through zero when the plane of the loop first becomes parallel to the field. It reaches a negative maximum after a quarter of a turn and returns to $+BA$ after one full revolution, so the graph is a cosine curve.

That is graph A. Graph B, starting from zero, would only apply if the plane of the loop were parallel to the field at $t = 0$; C and D do not vary continuously at all, which no rotating loop can produce. A useful check: the induced emf is proportional to the gradient of the flux graph, so a cosine flux curve means the emf is momentarily zero at $t = 0$ and largest as the flux crosses zero, even though the flux itself is then at its extremes.

items: 1 mark: recognises that with the plane of the loop perpendicular to the field the flux is at a maximum and varies sinusoidally, so the induced emf is momentarily zero at $t = 0$ (option A).

content.text: Brush X touches the metal axle and Brush Y touches the rim of the disc. If the metal disc is rotated uniformly as shown, which statement about the current through the globe is correct?
No current flows.
A direct current flows from Y to X.
A direct current flows from X to Y.
An alternating current flows between X and Y.
Decide whether the emf induced in a disc turning steadily about its axle in a steady field reverses direction during a single revolution.
Then use $F = qvB$ on a charge in the rim: the field runs from the N pole to the S pole, and the arrow on the disc fixes the direction of $v$.
B

The field in the gap between the poles runs from the N pole to the S pole, that is, across the disc and along the direction of its axle. The free electrons in the disc move with the metal as it turns, so each one has a velocity $v$ and experiences the magnetic force $F = evB$, which is perpendicular to both $v$ and $B$.

Because the field is along the axle, that force is directed radially in the plane of the disc, with the same sense at every point of the rim. It drives positive charge out to the rim and leaves negative charge on the axle, so Brush Y on the rim sits at a higher potential than Brush X on the axle, and the current in the external circuit flows from Y, through the globe, to X.

The sense of the force does not reverse as the disc rotates, so the emf keeps a single sign and the current is direct rather than alternating. That is response B. An alternating current, option D, is what a coil generator produces, where the direction of the force changes twice in every revolution; here the geometry of the disc does not change.

items: 1 mark: identifies that a direct current flows from Y to X (option B). As the disc rotates uniformly the direction of the motional emf in the disc is constant, so the current in the external circuit is unidirectional.

The data logger software displays the results as a pair of voltage–time graphs on a computer monitor. Which pair of graphs best depicts the student's results?

Option B: voltage–time graph for coil X shows two positive spikes; voltage–time graph for coil Y shows two positive spikes.
Option C: voltage–time graph for coil X shows a trapezoidal pulse; voltage–time graph for coil Y shows a flat-bottomed negative rectangular pulse.
Option D: voltage–time graph for coil X shows a sinusoidal waveform; voltage–time graph for coil Y shows a sinusoidal waveform.

content.text: Sketch what the voltage across the primary coil X does when the switch is closed and then opened, given that the supply is a single cell.
The secondary only responds while the flux in the core is changing, so mark on your sketch the two instants at which that happens.
A

Coil X is connected to a cell through a switch, so the voltage across X steps up to the full cell voltage when the switch closes, holds at that constant value, and falls back to zero when the switch is opened. The graph for X is therefore a flat-topped pulse, as shown in A, C and D.

The flux in the core is proportional to the primary current. While the switch is closed and that current is steady, the flux is constant, so $\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 0$ and no emf is induced in Y at all. A brief emf appears only at the two instants when the flux changes: a pulse as the switch closes and a pulse of the opposite polarity as it opens.

Since the secondary voltage is proportional to the rate of change of flux, Y shows two short spikes of opposite sign while X shows the sustained pulse, which is the pair of graphs in A. Option C is wrong because a sustained secondary voltage would require a sustained changing flux, and option D is wrong because the supply is a cell, not an a.c. source.

content.text: Lawrence and William Bragg used X-rays to determine the crystal structure of materials. Which property of waves was the basis of their technique?
Diffraction
Dispersion
Polarisation
Rarefaction

X-rays have a wavelength of the same order as the spacing between atoms in a crystal lattice. Which wave behaviour becomes significant when the repeating structure has a spacing comparable to the wavelength, and which wave property do the Bragg builders use to measure that spacing?
A

X-rays have a wavelength of about $0.1$ to $1\,\mathrm{nm}$, comparable to the spacing between atoms in a crystal. Waves diffract strongly when they meet a repeating structure whose spacing is comparable to the wavelength, so the regularly spaced layers of atoms in the crystal act as a three-dimensional diffraction grating.

Rays reflected from successive atomic planes travel different distances and interfere constructively at angles satisfying $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$. Measuring those angles, and knowing $\lambda$, gives the plane spacing $d$, and from that the crystal structure. The technique is based on diffraction. Dispersion (C in wavelength) and polarisation are not involved at all, and rarefaction is a feature of longitudinal waves such as sound, not of X-rays.

items: 1 mark: identifies diffraction of X-rays by crystal lattice planes as the basis of the Bragg technique (option A).

content.text: A charged non-magnetic particle is moving in a magnetic field. What would NOT affect the magnetic force on the particle?
The strength of the magnetic field
The magnitude of the charge on the particle
The velocity component parallel to the magnetic field direction
The velocity component perpendicular to the magnetic field direction
Write the force on a moving charge as $F = qvB\sin\theta$ and identify which component of the particle's velocity appears in $\theta$.
C
The force on a charge moving in a uniform magnetic field is $F = qvB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the velocity and the field.

Only the component of velocity perpendicular to the field contributes. Writing the velocity as a sum of components, the component parallel to $\mathbf{B}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{B}$, so $\mathbf{v}_\parallel \times \mathbf{B} = 0$ and it exerts no force whatsoever; the perpendicular component is what bends the path into a circle.

The magnitude of the force therefore does not depend on the velocity component parallel to the field, whereas it is directly proportional to $B$, to $q$ and to $v_\perp$. That is response C, and it is the reason a non-magnetic charged particle can drift along a field line without being accelerated.

items: 1 mark: identifies that only the velocity component perpendicular to the field enters $F = qvB\sin\theta$, so the parallel component does not affect the force (option C).

content.text: The temperature of a metal is reduced. Which statement correctly identifies the change in its electrical resistance and the reason for this change?
Increases — Metal freezes
Decreases — More free electrons available
Increases — Electrons move more slowly
Decreases — Reduced metal lattice vibrations
In a metal the conduction electrons are scattered by the vibrating positive ions of the lattice, so the resistance is set by how much those ions vibrate.
Decide what happens to the ion vibration as the metal is cooled, and hence how often the electrons are scattered.
D

In a metal the conduction electrons move freely through the lattice but are repeatedly scattered by the vibrating positive ions. It is the average time between these collisions that limits the drift speed of the electrons, and therefore the current for a given voltage.

Cooling the metal reduces the amplitude of the lattice vibrations, so the ions move less and the electrons are scattered less often. The mean time between collisions increases, so the electrons reach a higher drift speed under the same electric field and the resistance of the metal falls.

The resistance therefore decreases because the lattice vibrations are reduced, which is response D. The number of free electrons is essentially unchanged by cooling, so B is wrong, and a metal does not freeze at ordinary low temperatures, so A is wrong. C has the wrong direction of change as well as a faulty reason: the electrons do not simply move more slowly, they move faster on average.

items: 1 mark: identifies that cooling reduces metal lattice vibrations so fewer electron–positive ion collisions occur and the resistance decreases (option D).

C
For a uniform field between parallel plates, $E = \frac{V}{d}$. The original arrangement of $50\,\mathrm{V}$ across $10\,\mathrm{mm}$ gives
The new arrangement must therefore give $10\,000\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ with conducting plates, so that charge can be held on the surfaces:

Consider what could accelerate the projectile horizontally. Once it has left the launch point the only force acting is gravity, and gravity acts vertically.

The two components are perpendicular, so the launch velocity is the hypotenuse of the right triangle they form, and the components are the two shorter sides.

Because the projectile lands level with the point it was launched from, the upward part of the flight takes the same time as the downward part, so the total time of flight is twice the time to the top.
The range is then the constant horizontal velocity multiplied by that total time, not by the time to the top.

content.text: Parts of a space mission involve a spacecraft spending time in geostationary orbit, and then returning safely to Earth. Analyse the forces acting on this spacecraft during these parts of the mission.
Split the mission into the two stages the question names and treat them separately, because the forces and the resulting motion are not the same in each.

In stable orbit, draw the forces on the craft. The gravitational force and the 'centripetal force' are not two separate forces that cancel each other — establish the relationship between them and say what that implies about the speed and the radius.

For the return, describe in order what the thrusters do to the speed and hence to the orbital radius, what happens as the craft meets progressively denser atmosphere, and which force then does most of the work of bringing it down.

In geostationary orbit the only significant force is Earth's gravitational attraction, which provides the centripetal force, so the spacecraft travels at constant speed in a fixed radius. To re-enter, thrusters are fired opposite the direction of motion to reduce speed and hence total energy and orbital radius, then atmospheric drag slows the craft further and gravity brings it down to land.

During stable orbit the spacecraft has no net tangential force. The gravitational force $GMm/r^{2}$ acts radially inwards and exactly supplies the centripetal force $mv^{2}/r$ required, so the speed is constant and the two forces are not a balanced pair but a single inward resultant force. To return, thrusters fire opposite the direction of motion, decelerating the craft. Since total energy and orbital radius are related for a circular orbit, reducing the speed reduces the radius, so the craft descends into progressively denser atmosphere. Collisions with air particles then provide a frictional force opposite to the motion, which lowers the orbit further and dissipates energy as heat, while gravity pulls the craft back to land on Earth.

content.text: An object is stationary in space and located at a distance $10\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ from the centre of a certain planet. It is found that $1.0\,\mathrm{MJ}$ of work needs to be done to move the object to a stationary point $20\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ from the centre of the planet. Calculate how much more work needs to be done to move the object to a stationary point $80\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ from the centre of the planet.

Because $E_p = -GMm/r$ varies as $1/r$, the work needed for each doubling of distance is not the same. Work with one unknown constant such as $A = GMm$ instead of trying to find $G$ and the two masses separately.
Use the given $1.0\,\mathrm{MJ}$ to eliminate that constant from the first step, then ask how the work from $20\,000$ km out to $80\,000$ km compares with the work over the first interval.

Read the wording carefully: it asks for the work in addition to the $1.0\,\mathrm{MJ}$ already quoted, not the total over the whole journey. Check your result against the total work that would be needed to move the object all the way out to infinity.
$0.75\,\mathrm{MJ}$ of additional work

Because $E_p \propto -1/r$, the potential energy varies inversely with distance from the planet. Let $A = GMm$. Then $E_{p1} = -A/10\,000$, $E_{p2} = -A/20\,000$ and $E_{p3} = -A/80\,000$, with the distances in km.

Note that the total work done in moving the object all the way from $10\,000$ km to $80\,000$ km is $1.0 + 0.75 = 1.75\,\mathrm{MJ}$, which is less than the $2.0\,\mathrm{MJ}$ that would be needed to reach infinity. The question asks for the extra work beyond the $1.0\,\mathrm{MJ}$ already quoted, i.e. the $0.75\,\mathrm{MJ}$ needed to go from $20\,000$ km to $80\,000$ km.

1 mark: correct intermediate working: $W_{2 \to 3} = E_{p3} - E_{p2} = -\frac{A}{80\,000} + \frac{A}{20\,000} = \frac{3A}{80\,000}$
1 mark: correct final answer, $0.75\,\mathrm{MJ}$ of additional work, with correct units

content.text: Describe how the galvanometer operates as an application of the motor effect.

Identify the two forces the motor effect produces in the coil and where each one acts. Because they are equal and opposite on opposite sides of the coil, ask what they do to the rotation of the coil rather than to the motion of its centre.

The field between the pole pieces is radial, not parallel to the sides of the coil. Work out what that does to the size of the turning effect as the pointer swings across the scale, and why the design needs that property.

Finally, account for the role of the spring. It is what prevents the coil from rotating indefinitely, so its behaviour is what decides the relationship between the current and the size of the deflection.

Current in the coil placed in the radial magnetic field between the N and S pole pieces experiences forces on opposite sides of the coil, producing a constant torque that rotates the coil and turns the pointer against the restoring spring; the deflection is proportional to the current.

When current flows through the coil the motor effect produces equal and opposite forces on the two sides of the coil. Because the field in the gap between the pole pieces is radial, those forces always act perpendicular to the radius, so they produce a constant torque on the coil and no net sideways force. The coil, with the soft iron core attached to it, rotates and carries the pointer with it across the scale. The spring provides a restoring torque proportional to the deflection, so equilibrium is reached when the driving torque equals the restoring torque and the deflection is proportional to the current. This is why the galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter by adding a suitable shunt or series resistance.

content.text: Identify the relative directions of the currents in both rods, and justify your answer.
Decide whether the magnetic force on the lower rod pushes it onto the balance or lifts it off, and then use the change in the reading to work out which of those is happening.
A falling reading means the balance is supporting less of the rod’s weight, so something other than the balance is now carrying part of that weight.

Then use the standard result for two long parallel conductors: like currents attract, unlike currents repel. Work from the direction of the force to the direction of the currents, not the other way round.
The currents flow in the **same direction** in both rods.

The balance reading decreases as the current in the lower rod increases, so the balance is supporting less of the rod's weight and the magnetic force on the lower rod must be directed upwards, towards the upper rod. The rods therefore attract each other, and parallel currents flowing in the same direction attract, so the currents must be in the same direction.

The balance reading falls from $0.5485\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $2.8\,\mathrm{A}$ to $0.5465\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $20.0\,\mathrm{A}$, so the magnetic force on the lower rod grows with the current in that rod and is directed upwards, lifting the rod partly off the balance and towards the upper rod. An upward force on the lower rod towards the upper rod means the two rods attract each other.

The force between two long parallel conductors is attractive when the currents are parallel, that is flowing in the same direction along the rods, and repulsive only when they are antiparallel. Since the rods attract, the currents in the two rods must be in the same direction. Had they been antiparallel the rods would repel, the lower rod would be pushed down onto the balance and the reading would increase, which is the opposite of what the data show.

List the applications first, then for each one state the property that makes it possible — zero electrical resistance, or expulsion of magnetic flux — and the practical consequence of that property.
Do not stop at listing benefits. The question asks about both society and the environment, and for any technology you must weigh at least one cost against the benefits.
A full response ends with a value judgement that is supported by the impacts already described: say explicitly which impacts you are weighing and why you reached that conclusion.

Overall, the potential applications of superconductors — maglev trains, lossless power transmission and more efficient power generation and medical imaging — would benefit both society and the environment, but the high cost of implementation and the large energy required to keep superconductors below their critical temperature currently prevent widespread adoption.

Superconductors, cooled below a critical temperature, have zero electrical resistance and expel magnetic flux (the Meissner effect). Potential applications include maglev trains, giving frictionless transport at very high speed; superconducting power cables, allowing large-scale transmission of electricity with no $I^2R$ losses; superconducting generators, removing the need for AC and large transformers; and very strong magnets for medical imaging and particle accelerators. For society these mean faster, more energy-efficient transport, cheaper and more reliable electricity supply and more powerful diagnostic equipment. For the environment they mean less fossil fuel burnt for power generation and so less atmospheric pollution and acid rain. However, the materials are expensive, fabrication and maintenance costs are high, there is no technology yet to maintain a large superconducting distribution grid, and cooling to the critical temperature (often with liquid helium) consumes a large amount of energy which is itself usually generated from fossil fuels. Judged overall the applications are advantageous to both society and the environment, provided the cost and cooling-energy problems can be overcome in the future.

content.text: Explain the physics responsible for this observation.
The block is a conductor and the magnet's flux through it is changing, so currents are induced in closed loops inside the block. Name them and say what field they produce.

The direction rule fixes everything that follows: the field of the induced currents opposes the change that produced them, so decide whether the resulting force on the falling magnet is up or down, and what that does to the magnet's kinetic energy.

As the magnet approaches the copper block, the changing magnetic flux through the block induces eddy currents. By Lenz's law the field of these induced currents opposes the change in flux, so the force on the magnet is upwards and opposes its motion, slowing it until it lands gently.

The copper block is a conductor. As the magnet approaches, the magnetic flux through the block changes, so an emf is induced and eddy currents circulate within the block in closed loops. By Lenz's law the direction of these induced currents is such that the magnetic field they produce opposes the change in flux that caused them — here, the approach of the magnet. The magnet therefore experiences a force directed upwards, opposing its downward motion. This slows the magnet as it approaches the block, so it lands gently rather than striking the copper hard. A block of a more strongly conducting material would produce larger eddy currents and so a greater opposing force.

content.text: Predict what will happen if the experiment is repeated with a copper block cooled to approximately $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Justify your prediction.
First check whether $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is anywhere near the critical temperature of copper, because that decides whether the block is still an ordinary conductor or has become superconducting.

Then ask what cooling does to the resistance of a metal, and what the smaller resistance does to the eddy currents driven by the same induced emf. Both the prediction and its justification follow from that chain, so a sudden change in behaviour should not be expected at this temperature.
The magnet will slow down more than in part (a) and land even more gently.

Cooling the copper to $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ decreases its electrical resistance (it is still far above copper's critical temperature of about $-196^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), so the same induced emf drives larger eddy currents whose stronger field produces a greater retarding force.

Copper's critical temperature is about $-196^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so at $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the copper is still an ordinary conductor — it is not superconducting and the Meissner effect does not apply. However, cooling reduces the lattice vibrations in the copper and therefore its electrical resistance. The induced emf driving the eddy currents is unchanged, so the larger currents produce a stronger associated magnetic field and hence a greater force opposing the falling magnet. The magnet therefore slows down more than it did at room temperature.

content.text: Draw labelled diagrams of the band structures of an insulator, a semiconductor, and a conductor.
Sketch each material as a pair of horizontal lines for the allowed energy bands, with electron energy increasing upward and the filled band at the bottom of the drawing.

Then change only one thing from one diagram to the next: the size of the gap between the top of the filled band and the next band, and whether the two bands touch at all. Label each diagram so the later parts can be answered from them.

Insulator: a filled valence band separated from an empty conduction band by a large energy gap. Semiconductor: a filled valence band separated from an empty conduction band by a small gap. Conductor: the valence band overlaps the conduction band (or the conduction band is partly filled).

In each diagram the vertical axis is electron energy and the horizontal lines are bands of allowed energies. For an insulator the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, separated by a large energy gap, so electrons cannot be promoted at ordinary temperatures. For a semiconductor the same two bands exist but with a much smaller gap, so a few electrons are thermally promoted into the conduction band. For a conductor the highest occupied band is only partly filled, so the valence and conduction bands overlap and free electrons are always available.

items: 2 marks: diagrams have conduction and valence bands, and a suitable gap between.

content.text: With reference to your diagrams, describe the differences in electrical resistance between insulators, semiconductors and conductors.

Compare the three diagrams you drew rather than describing the materials in general. The thing that differs between them is the size of the energy gap, and the gap is what decides how many electrons reach the conduction band at a given temperature.
Once you have the number of charge carriers for each material, ask what that does to the resistance, and make sure all three cases are covered in the same order as the diagrams.

Insulators: high electrical resistance as a large amount of energy is required to move electrons into the conduction band. Semiconductors: medium resistance as the energy gap is smaller and therefore less energy is needed to move electrons across it. Conductors: low resistance as in the diagram the valence band is the same as the conduction band.

Comparing the diagrams, the insulator has the largest band gap, so the greatest energy is required to promote electrons into the conduction band and very few charge carriers exist, so the resistance is high. The semiconductor has a smaller gap, so fewer electrons need promotion and more carriers are available, giving an intermediate resistance. The conductor's bands overlap, so the conduction band is already partly filled and electrons move freely, giving a very low resistance.

content.text: Explain how the addition of trace amounts of certain elements, such as phosphorus, can change the electrical resistance of semiconductors at a given temperature.
Identify where silicon and the dopant sit in the periodic table and count the valence electrons each contributes to the lattice when it forms bonds.

Then ask what becomes of the extra electron. It is only weakly bound, so it can be promoted into the conduction band easily, and at the same temperature that means far more charge carriers are available than before — which is the quantity that sets the resistance.

Doping with phosphorus, which has five valence electrons compared with four in silicon, adds extra free electrons to the conduction band, increasing the number of charge carriers, so the resistance of the semiconductor decreases at that temperature.

Adding trace phosphorus to silicon replaces some silicon atoms in the lattice. Phosphorus has one more valence electron than silicon, so each dopant atom contributes an extra electron that is only weakly bound and is promoted easily to the conduction band. At a given temperature the number of free charge carriers is therefore much greater, so the semiconductor's electrical resistance decreases. Adding a Group II element instead would create holes, with the same effect on the resistance.

content.text: Discuss the origins of unwanted heat production in transformers and ways in which these can be overcome.

Separate the sources of heat before you look for fixes. One is associated with the changing magnetic flux in the core and the other with the current in the windings, and they need different solutions.

For the core, ask what the induced eddy currents have to do with the resistance of the iron, and how building the core from thin sheets separated by insulating layers changes the resistance of the current paths.
The marking scheme requires TWO valid strategies, so make sure your second one addresses the heating of the windings rather than repeating the first.

Unwanted heating arises from eddy currents induced in the soft iron core by the changing magnetic flux and from $I^2R$ heating of the coil windings. Eddy currents are reduced by laminating the core, and coil heating is reduced by using thicker, lower-resistance wire or a coolant such as oil or water.

In a transformer the primary current is alternating, so the flux in the core changes continuously. This changing flux induces eddy currents in the soft iron core, and the resistance of the core converts their energy into heat. This is overcome by laminating the core — building it from thin sheets of soft iron separated by insulating layers — which greatly increases the resistance of the eddy current loops and so reduces the current flowing in them. In addition, current flowing in the primary and secondary windings heats those wires because of their resistance. This is overcome by using thicker wire, which has a lower resistance, or by cooling the transformer with oil or water. Two valid strategies are therefore laminating the core and using thicker wires or a coolant.

1 mark: states eddy current production, OR states heating in windings due to current flow, OR outlines a strategy for heat reduction.

content.text: Outline the roles of the deflection plates and the electrodes in the electron gun.
Work along the tube in the direction the electrons travel and deal with one stage at a time: source, accelerating and focusing electrodes, then the plate pairs, then the screen.

For each stage name what it does to the beam rather than what it looks like — emit, speed up, make parallel, turn sideways, display. The mark is for the roles being distinguished, so keep the gun electrodes and the deflection plates as two separate groups.

The cathode, anode and focusing electrodes in the electron gun emit, accelerate and focus the electrons into a narrow parallel beam; the pairs of deflection plates then apply transverse electric fields that deflect the beam horizontally and vertically so the spot traces the signal on the fluorescent screen.

The heated cathode releases electrons by thermionic emission. The anode and other electrodes are held at higher potential, so they accelerate the electrons, while the focusing electrodes shape them into a narrow, parallel beam travelling along the tube axis. After the beam has passed through the electron gun it enters the region of the vertical deflection plates, where a potential difference applied across those plates creates a horizontal electric field that deflects the beam sideways; the horizontal plates similarly deflect it vertically. The amount of deflection is proportional to the plate voltage, so the beam traces a graph of a changing voltage on the fluorescent screen.

content.text: Beginning in the late 19th century, observations and experiments on black body radiation and the photoelectric effect led physicists to revise their existing model of light. Use the above as an example to explain how scientists test and validate models.
A model earns acceptance by making quantitative predictions that can be tested, so start with the specific prediction that each of the two investigations was designed to check.

State the two observational failures precisely: what classical wave theory predicted for the black body curves, and what it wrongly predicted for the photoelectric effect, including the threshold frequency and the linear relationship between maximum kinetic energy and frequency.
Close the loop by saying what the replacement model predicted instead, and use the fact that it reproduced both sets of measured data to justify calling it validated rather than merely proposed.

Scientists made quantitative predictions from the wave model of light and tested them against precise experiments. Black body measurements showed the classical prediction failed at short wavelengths, and the photoelectric effect showed light ejects electrons only above a threshold frequency with kinetic energy increasing linearly with frequency. Because the results repeatedly disagreed with the accepted model, the model was rejected and a new quantum model with $E = hf$ was proposed and shown to match both sets of observations.

A scientific model is validated by deriving quantitative predictions from it and comparing those predictions with carefully controlled, repeatable measurements; a model is not accepted merely because it is elegant. In the late 19th century the wave model of light, combined with classical mechanics and thermodynamics, predicted that a black body would emit ever more energy as the wavelength decreased, diverging violently from the measured black body curves. Similarly the wave model predicted that light of any frequency and intensity should eject electrons from a metal, yet experiments on the photoelectric effect showed a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted and that the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases linearly with frequency, independent of intensity. These repeatable, controlled experimental results contradicted specific quantitative predictions of the accepted model, so the model was invalidated in those domains and a new model in which light consists of photons of energy $E = hf$ was proposed. That new model successfully predicted the observed black body curves and the linear photoelectric relationships, so it was validated and adopted in place of the old model.

content.text: Describe ONE subsequent observation that led other scientists to argue that cathode rays were charged particles.
Electromagnetic radiation carries no charge, so it would be undeflected by a field. Any observation that depends on the ray's charge or on its mass therefore discriminates between the two models.

Describe both the procedure and what was seen, including the direction of any deflection, since it is the direction that identifies the sign of the charge. A magnetic field deflecting the rays, or a paddle wheel being spun by them, are equally valid observations.
Cathode rays were deflected towards the positively charged plate and repelled by the negatively charged plate when electric fields were applied, showing that the rays carry negative charge.

Accept alternatives: deflection of the rays by a magnetic field in the direction expected for negatively charged particles; or rotation of a paddle wheel placed in the path of the rays, showing they have momentum and hence mass.

Thomson placed the discharge tube between charged plates and observed that the cathode ray beam bent towards the positive plate and away from the negative plate. A stream of electromagnetic radiation is electrically neutral and would not be deflected, so the deflection shows that the rays carry charge; because the beam bends towards the positive plate the charge must be negative. Equally valid observations are the deflection of the rays by a magnetic field in the direction expected for negatively charged particles, and the rotation of a small paddle wheel placed in the path of the rays, which shows the rays possess momentum and therefore mass.

General advice such as 'be careful' does not earn the mark; for example, shielding the tube and viewing through the small window controls the radiation hazard, and isolating the supply controls the electrical hazard.

Hazard: exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the discharge tube, which can damage the eyes and skin. Safe work practice: shield the tube in a light-proof case and view it only through the small viewing window, keeping the shutters closed at all other times.

Gas discharge tubes emit intense ultraviolet radiation, which can cause photochemical damage to the eyes and skin, so the tube must be enclosed in a light-proof case and viewed only through the small viewing window, with the shutters closed when not in use. Alternatively the electrical hazard from the high-voltage supply can be accepted, addressed by switching off and isolating the supply before adjusting the tube.

Interpreting the anomalies. The free-air and latitude corrections account for the fact that the field is weaker at the poles and higher with altitude, and the Bouguer correction subtracts the pull of the rock lying between a station and datum elevation using an assumed rock density. content.text: Seismic wave reflection and refraction, and the path of seismic waves through Earth.

For (i), think about what a marker looks for in a survey that times waves over a fixed line: the same source energy, the same geophone positions each time, more than one reading per station, and a graph rather than a single number.

For (ii), trace each ray in the diagram and ask why it is bent rather than straight. Then ask which of the two wave types could travel through the fluid outer core — the answer explains both the shape of the S-type path and the band of distances over which P-waves go missing.
Refraction, not insensitivity, causes the missing P-waves: at the core-mantle boundary the seismic velocity jumps, so rays are bent steeply downwards and miss the surface over a range of distances.

items: (b)(i) Reliability features: the same source was used with the same energy for every shot; geophones were placed at fixed, equally spaced stations and kept firmly coupled to the ground; several readings were taken at each station and the arrival times averaged; identical readings were discarded as outliers; arrival times were plotted as a graph against station distance and a best-fit line drawn, so the slope (and hence the velocity and the depth) came from many measurements rather than one.

(b)(ii) Rays are curved because seismic velocity increases with depth, so a ray crossing successive layers is continuously refracted; the rays are arcs of circles centred on the Earth's centre and they turn back towards the surface.

(b)(ii) At the core-mantle boundary the velocity rises from about $8\,\mathrm{km/s}$ in the mantle to about $13\,\mathrm{km/s}$ in the outer core, so rays entering the core are bent steeply away from the normal. This produces a P-wave shadow zone from about $103^{\circ}$ to $142^{\circ}$; P-waves reappear beyond $142^{\circ}$ after being refracted by the solid inner core, whose higher velocity turns them back to the surface.

(b)(ii) S-type waves cannot pass through a liquid, so the S-type ray in the diagram stops at the core-mantle boundary and no S-waves are recorded beyond about $103^{\circ}$ from the epicentre (the S-wave shadow zone). This absence is the primary evidence that the outer core, from about $2900\,\mathrm{km}$ to $5150\,\mathrm{km}$ depth, is liquid.

content.text: Part (i). A refraction survey measures the arrival time of the first (direct or head) wave at each geophone. The random errors that matter are the uncertainty in reading the arrival time off the trace and small differences in ground coupling. The response is to average repeated readings at each station, keep the geometry and source energy constant, and replace any single measurement with a value taken from a straight-line fit of time against distance. The gradient of that line is $1/v$, so the velocity comes from the whole line of data, and the intercept gives the depth of the refracting layer.

Part (ii), curvature of the paths. Seismic velocity is not constant: it rises with depth because both density and elastic modulus increase. Applying Snell's law to each boundary between layers of different velocity gives

so the ray bends towards the normal on entering faster material. Because the increase is gradual rather than a single interface, the ray is bent continuously and follows a smooth circular arc, turning back towards the surface when it reaches its turning point. That is why the paths in the diagram are arcs and not straight lines.

Part (ii), the liquid outer core. S-type waves are shear waves: they require a medium that can support a shear stress, which a liquid cannot. Hence the S-type ray in the diagram ends at the core-mantle boundary, and beyond about $103^{\circ}$ from the epicentre no S-waves arrive at all. P-type waves are compressional waves and do travel through liquids, but they travel much faster there ($13\,\mathrm{km/s}$ compared with $8\,\mathrm{km/s}$ in the mantle), so on entering the core they are refracted steeply away from the normal. Over the range of distances for which every possible ray is turned downwards, no P-wave reaches the surface: the P-wave shadow zone from about $103^{\circ}$ to $142^{\circ}$. Beyond $142^{\circ}$ the rays are turned back by refraction at the inner-core boundary, where the velocity rises again, which is why P-waves reappear there. The existence of both shadow zones, measured worldwide, is what allows the liquid outer core and the solid inner core to be inferred.

content.text: 'Our understanding of Earth has changed as a result of developments in geophysics.' Discuss this statement with reference to the geophysical methods you have studied.
Open with an explicit judgement on the statement, then organise the whole body around two methods only. The marking notes reward two methods treated in detail rather than four mentioned in passing.

For each method give the chain: what the early technique could measure, the specific development that changed it (an instrument, a computing method or a theory), and the specific new knowledge that followed. The link between the development and the knowledge is where the marks are, not the list of instruments.

Close by returning to the judgement and giving one genuine limitation of both methods together. A balanced conclusion scores above an unqualified one, and coherence and logical progression are marked separately from content.

Judgement: the statement is well supported. Improved instrumentation and computing have transformed both the seismic and gravity methods, so that Earth is now understood as a dynamic, layered planet rather than a static ball.

Seismic methods: originally seismographs recorded only the arrival times of P- and S-waves so that distant earthquakes could be located. Once digital recording, many seismograph stations and modern computer travel-time tomography were introduced, the arrival times from all around the world could be combined to map the interior. This revealed the liquid outer core from the S-wave shadow zone, the solid inner core, and convection in the mantle — knowledge that changed our view of Earth from a static layered ball to a dynamic planet with a geodynamo. Gravity methods: early gravity surveys used simple pendulums and their readings were dominated by latitude, elevation and the mass of rock above the station. The development of gravimeters accurate to a fraction of a mgal, aircraft and satellite altimetry, and computer-based reduction with latitude, free air and Bouguer corrections made it possible to map subsurface density contrasts. Airborne and satellite gravity now map the oceanic crust and continental margins, confirming plate-tectonic models. Overall the statement is justified: these two methods now underpin modern plate tectonics, though the resolution of the deep interior is still limited and the methods cannot detect very small or very deep features.

content.text: Paleomagnetic patterns in the seabed and the calculation of sea-floor spreading rate.

A stripe records one interval of constant polarity. Work out what happens to the iron minerals in basalt at the instant it cools below the Curie point, and what has to be true of the field for a stripe to be laid down.
The stripes are symmetric about the ridge, so measure a boundary on whichever side of the ridge is drawn more clearly, and use the polarity time scale to convert each stripe into an age.

Rate is distance divided by age, with the age in millions of years. Calculate it for at least two boundaries: if the spreading rate is uniform, the answers should agree, and that agreement is itself the check that the boundaries have been matched to the right ages.

items: (d)(i) As basalt solidifies at the ridge its temperature falls below the Curie point and the iron oxide minerals it contains become permanently magnetised along the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at that instant, so each newly formed strip of sea floor is stamped with the polarity in force when it cooled. Whenever the field reverses, the next strip is stamped with the opposite polarity, producing alternating normal and reversed stripes. New crust is continuously created at the ridge and carried away on both sides by sea-floor spreading, so a stripe and its mirror image lie the same distance from the ridge, and the oldest crust is furthest away. Cooling of the crust at depth also leaves a remanent magnetisation aligned with the present field, which is why rocks of all ages on land show the same pattern of reversals.

(d)(ii) Rate $= \dfrac{\text{distance from the ridge}}{\text{age}}$. The $0.73\,\mathrm{Myr}$ boundary lies about $19\,\mathrm{mm}$ from the ridge on the diagram scale and the $1.67\,\mathrm{Myr}$ boundary about $44\,\mathrm{mm}$, giving $26.4$ and $26.3\,\mathrm{mm}$ per million years respectively; the $0.90\,\mathrm{Myr}$ boundary at about $24\,\mathrm{mm}$ gives $27.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ per million years. The rate is therefore constant at about $26\,\mathrm{mm}$ per million years on one side of the ridge, i.e. about $2.6\,\mathrm{cm}$ per year if the horizontal axis scale is $1\,\mathrm{mm} = 10\,\mathrm{km}$ (full spreading rate about $5.2\,\mathrm{cm/yr}$).

content.text: Part (i), how the stripes form. Basaltic magma erupts at the ridge, and as the lava cools through the Curie temperature of its magnetic minerals those minerals lock in a permanent magnetisation parallel to the Earth's field at that moment. A change in the lava that is now cooling produces a new strip with the opposite magnetisation if the field has reversed in the meantime, and none if it has not. The result is a set of alternating normal and reversed bands lying parallel to the ridge, whose ages increase outwards. Because the same process runs on both sides of the ridge, each band has a mirror image at the same distance on the opposite side, and the sequence of bands outwards is identical on both sides — the symmetry of the profile in the diagram is direct evidence that the crust is being created at the ridge and moved away from it.

Part (ii), measuring the boundaries. The polarity time scale gives four boundaries in the interval shown, at $0.73$, $0.90$, $0.97$ and $1.67\,\mathrm{Myr}$. The profile is symmetric, so each boundary is placed where the trace changes between a positive and a negative anomaly; measuring on the clearer side and averaging the two sides removes half the reading error.

The three independent boundaries give the same value to within about 3 per cent, so the spreading has been at a constant rate of roughly $26\,\mathrm{mm}$ per million years on each side of the ridge over the last $1.67\,\mathrm{Myr}$. Converting with the axis scale of the diagram ($1\,\mathrm{mm} = 10\,\mathrm{km}$) gives about $260\,\mathrm{km}$ of new crust per million years, i.e. $2.6\,\mathrm{cm/yr}$ on one side and about $5.2\,\mathrm{cm/yr}$ for the two sides combined, which is a typical fast-spreading mid-ocean ridge.

content.text: The acoustic impedance and density of a number of different types of body tissue, ultrasound gel and air are shown in the table.
The speed of a wave is not given directly: divide the acoustic impedance by the density. Do this for more than one material and check that the answers are of a sensible order before going further.

For the reflection question use the reflection coefficients at a boundary between two media. The intensity coefficient is the square of the amplitude coefficient, so a small mismatch in impedance produces a very much smaller mismatch in intensity.

Compare the impedance mismatch at the fat-air boundary with the mismatch at the fat-gel boundary. Whatever survives that comparison is the reason gel is applied to the skin, and the same comparison explains why an air gap cannot be tolerated between probe and patient.

items: (a)(i) Using $v = Z/\rho$: fat $\dfrac{1.38\times10^{6}}{9.25\times10^{2}} = 1.49\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$; skin $\dfrac{1.52\times10^{6}}{1.00\times10^{3}} = 1.52\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$; gel $\dfrac{1.54\times10^{6}}{1.01\times10^{3}} = 1.52\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$; air $\dfrac{4.0\times10^{2}}{1.3} = 3.1\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

(a)(ii) Ultrasound is only useful where it can enter the body and bounce off a boundary, and the fraction reflected depends on the impedance mismatch. At the fat-air boundary, $\left(\dfrac{0.0004 - 1.38}{0.0004 + 1.38}\right)^{2} = 0.999$, so $99.9\,\%$ of the intensity is reflected and essentially none enters the patient. Because the air gap between probe and skin has almost the wrong impedance, every air pocket would completely block the image. Ultrasound gel has an impedance of $1.54$, very close to skin's $1.52$, so the gel-skin boundary reflects only $\left(\dfrac{1.52 - 1.54}{1.52 + 1.54}\right)^{2} = 1.1\times10^{-4}$ and the fat-gel boundary only $\left(\dfrac{1.54 - 1.38}{1.54 + 1.38}\right)^{2} = 3.0\times10^{-3}$, i.e. $0.30\,\%$. Filling the air layer with gel therefore raises the transmitted intensity from a negligible fraction to about $99.7\,\%$, removes the multiple reflections that would obscure the returning echoes, and couples the probe mechanically as well as acoustically. The same reasoning explains why gel also removes air from the imaging window.

content.text: Part (i). Acoustic impedance is $Z = \rho v$, so it contains the wave speed directly. Rearranging gives $v = Z/\rho$, and the values are physically sensible for all four materials, which is the check that the tabulated impedances are of the order $10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}s^{-1}}$.
Part (ii). At a boundary between media 1 and 2 the amplitude reflection coefficient is $(Z_2 - Z_1)/(Z_2 + Z_1)$ and the fraction of intensity reflected is its square.

Substituting gel for air drops the reflected fraction from $99.9\,\%$ to $0.30\,\%$, a factor of about 3300, so almost the whole pulse is transmitted into the tissue and the returning echoes are not swamped by echoes from the air gap. That is the reason gel is applied, and it is also why air is fatal between the probe and the patient and why air must be removed from any imaging field (a lung, the bowel gas, or the amniotic fluid interface).

content.text: During your study of Medical Physics you identified data sources, and gathered, processed and presented information to explain why MRI scans can be used to detect abnormalities in the body.

Part (i) is about MRI as a technique. Treat each characteristic as a separate criterion and give a feature for at least two of them, so that the response reads as a comparison against other imaging methods.
Part (ii) is about image contrast. Ask what a cancerous cell is doing with water and hydrogen nuclei that a healthy cell is not, and how that difference survives the trip back to the detector.

A magnetometer reading with no position information is not an image. Remember that the applied field is deliberately made to vary from place to place, and ask what that does to the frequency of the returning signal.

items: (b)(i) Characteristics and features: the sample is placed in a very strong static magnetic field (typically 1.5 to 3 T), which aligns the magnetic moments of the hydrogen nuclei in body water and fat as parallel or antiparallel; a radio-frequency pulse at the resonance (Larmor) frequency $f = \gamma B/2\pi$, about 64 MHz at 1.5 T, tips the moments out of alignment and they then precess and give out a radio signal as they relax. Because it uses only radio waves and magnetic fields, MRI uses no ionising radiation and so carries no cancer risk, which is its decisive advantage for repeated imaging, for children and for pregnancy. Other criteria: contrast, because the signal depends on the density and the environment of the hydrogen nuclei, so soft tissue (brain, spinal cord, discs, tumour, muscle, fat) is separated far better than with X-rays; resolution and speed, with whole images in tens of minutes but real sensitivity to patient movement, so scan times are long; cost and space, with machines costing many times a CT scanner, needing RF shielding, a shielded room and superconducting cooling, so availability is limited to major hospitals; poor response to bone, lung and air-filled regions, which give almost no signal, so cortical bone is imaged far less well than with X-rays.

(b)(ii) Detection of cancerous tissue: a tumour differs from the surrounding healthy tissue in its water content and therefore in the number of hydrogen nuclei per unit volume and in their chemical environment. When the radio-frequency pulse is applied the nuclei in the tumour are therefore tipped and relax differently, and their precessing signal has a different intensity and a different decay time from the signal of healthy tissue. Because the main field is deliberately made to vary slightly across the sample (the gradient fields), the frequency of the returning signal is proportional to the field strength at the point it came from, and so the position of the emitting nuclei is encoded in the frequency of the signal; this is what turns the measurement into an image rather than a single number. The result is an image in which the tumour appears as a region of different brightness whose position, size and boundary can be read directly, allowing it to be located and measured. When the plain image is not conclusive, a gadolinium-based contrast agent is given: it is taken up preferentially by abnormal tissue and shortens the relaxation time there, making the tumour appear brighter and its margin sharper against the normal tissue.

content.text: Part (i). The signal that produces an MRI image is radio emission from the hydrogen nuclei of body water, not radiation absorbed from the patient. In the main field $B$ each nuclear magnetic moment precesses at the Larmor frequency

so with $\gamma/2\pi = 42.6\,\mathrm{MHz\,T^{-1}}$ a 1.5 T machine radiates at about $64\,\mathrm{MHz}$. A radio-frequency pulse at exactly this frequency is therefore resonant with the nuclei and tips them out of the equilibrium direction; on release they precess and induce a signal in a receiver coil, decaying with time constants $T_1$ and $T_2$ that depend on the molecular environment. This gives the criteria the marking notes ask for: radiation type (radio waves, so non-ionising), what is contrasted (the local density and environment of hydrogen nuclei, so excellent soft-tissue contrast), time (minutes, with sensitivity to motion), cost and space (shielded room, superconducting magnet, very high capital cost), and sensitivity (none to cortical bone or air).

Part (ii). Two effects separate tumour from healthy tissue. First, the relaxation behaviour: tumour tissue holds a different amount of water and a different density of hydrogen nuclei, so after the same radio-frequency pulse its spins dephase and rephase at a different rate, and its returning signal is stronger or weaker than that of the surrounding tissue. Second, the encoding of position: a gradient is superimposed on the main field so that the local field, and therefore the local Larmor frequency, differs from place to place,

so the frequency of a returning signal identifies the position it came from. Computer reconstruction of the intensity and frequency data gives an image in which the abnormal region appears with different contrast from healthy tissue, so its position, size and extent can be measured and a biopsy target chosen. Adding a gadolinium chelate shortens $T_1$ preferentially in abnormal tissue, increasing that contrast where it is needed.

content.text: Advances in our understanding of the electromagnetic spectrum have allowed scientists to investigate the human body in more detail. Assess the impact of these advances on the development of medical technologies.
Make the value judgement in the first sentence, then work through the four technologies the marking notes name, in that order, so the reader can follow the argument.

For each technology, state which property of the electromagnetic spectrum makes it work (penetrating power, wavelength, ionising energy) and what clinical problem that property solves. The notes require the spectrum to be explicitly linked, not merely named.

Before restating the judgement, weigh the two costs: capital and maintenance cost, which limits access, and ionising dose, which is a small real risk for X-ray, CAT and PET but absent for MRI and endoscopy.

Overall the advances in understanding the electromagnetic spectrum have had a strongly positive impact on medical technology, giving clinicians non-invasive, high-resolution images that have transformed diagnosis, although the equipment is expensive and the ionising techniques carry a small health risk.

Each region of the electromagnetic spectrum has properties that suit particular medical uses. X-rays and gamma rays have high penetrating power, so X-ray radiography gives quick images of bones, and the CAT scan combines many X-ray views taken from different angles by computer reconstruction, giving cross-sectional images of internal organs with much better contrast than plain X-rays. PET scans use positron-emitting radioisotopes whose emitted gamma rays are detected, so metabolic activity can be mapped and cancers located. Endoscopy uses visible light carried along fibre optic bundles, so the interior of the digestive tract can be examined and treated directly without surgery. MRI uses radio waves in the strong magnetic field, so it images hydrogen nuclei in body water with no ionising radiation at all and gives excellent soft-tissue contrast. Together these technologies have replaced exploratory surgery, allowed earlier and more accurate diagnosis and reduced patient risk. The negative impacts are the high capital and maintenance cost of MRI, CT and PET, which limits access, and the ionising radiation used by X-ray, CT and PET, which carries a small risk of inducing cancer. On balance the impact has been strongly positive and continues to improve as detectors and computing become more sensitive and less expensive.

content.text: Identify each image from what it records rather than from how it looks: one records the chemistry of the bone, one records its shape directly, and one is a computed reconstruction assembled from many projections.

For the comparison, choose criteria that apply to both techniques at once — cost, radiation dose, resolution, whether structures are superimposed, and what you can do with the result once you have it.

For the bone scan contrast, the decisive difference is that it images metabolic activity, so it can show disease while the bone still looks normal in shape. Say what that lets a clinician do earlier than with X-ray or CAT.

items: (d)(i) Image A is a bone scan, obtained by injecting a radioactive tracer (commonly technetium-99m attached to a phosphate compound) that is taken up wherever bone is being actively remodelled; image B is a plain X-ray radiograph; image C is a CAT (CT) scan, a cross-sectional image reconstructed by computer from many X-ray projections taken at different angles.

(d)(ii) X-ray versus CAT scan. Advantages of X-ray: a single exposure, cheap, fast, a small radiation dose, and it produces a projection image that a radiologist is highly experienced at reading. Disadvantages: it is a two-dimensional projection, so structures at different depths are superimposed and only one side of a structure can be seen; contrast between soft tissues is poor, so many soft-tissue abnormalities are invisible; the image records shape only. Advantages of CAT: computer reconstruction removes the superimposition, giving a true cross-section, so the position and depth of a fracture, a foreign body or an internal organ is known exactly; contrast between soft tissues is far better; the volume data can be viewed from any angle and reformatted in three dimensions; the attenuation values can be measured quantitatively. Disadvantages: many exposures are needed, so the ionising dose is substantially higher than for a single X-ray; the machine and its maintenance are far more expensive; the scan takes longer, so motion artefacts appear in restless or injured patients; and some patients cannot be scanned at all because of the weight limit or metal in the body.

(d)(iii) Bone scan contrasted with X-ray and CAT scan. A bone scan detects the gamma radiation emitted by the tracer, so it images how actively the bone is metabolising calcium, not the shape of the bone. Where bone is fractured, infected or infiltrated by metastatic cancer, new bone is being laid down and the tracer concentrates there, producing a hot spot. Because this happens within days of an injury or a secondary tumour, while the bone is still structurally normal, the scan becomes abnormal before anything can be seen on an X-ray or a CAT scan, and it shows many sites at once, which is exactly what is needed when searching for metastases. The price is anatomical detail: a bone scan has poor spatial resolution and no cross-section, so it shows that a lesion exists and roughly where, but not its shape or its relationship to nearby structures. It also requires an injection and takes one to three days for the tracer to accumulate, it is insensitive to purely mechanical problems that cause no bone turnover, and like X-ray and CAT it uses ionising radiation, so it is unsuitable for pregnancy and for frequent repeat use. X-ray and CAT give the complementary information: immediate, high-resolution pictures of structure, but nothing at all about the chemistry of the bone.

content.text: Identifying the images. A shows the diffuse, grainy appearance of a scintigram with a single intense focus in the palm and no visible bone structure, which is the signature of a gamma-emitting tracer (a bone scan). B shows bones as bright silhouettes against a dark background with the soft tissue almost invisible, which is a transmission radiograph, i.e. an X-ray. C shows individual carpal bones as separate bright shapes with clear boundaries in a cross-section, which can only be a reconstruction from many projections taken around the wrist, i.e. a CAT scan.

How each image is produced and what it therefore shows. X-ray and CAT both use absorption of high-energy photons, so both image the attenuation of tissue and both show structure. An X-ray records the sum of the attenuation along one line of sight, so everything is superimposed; a CAT acquires many such projections over a rotation of $360^{\circ}$ and reconstructs the attenuation distribution in a slice by computer, so there is no superimposition and the attenuation values can be measured. The bone scan instead detects $0.51\,\mathrm{MeV}$ gamma photons emitted after an internal conversion electron has cascaded down from technetium-99m, which has a half-life of about 6 hours and decays by gamma emission to molybdenum-99. The tracer chemises onto hydroxyapatite at sites of active bone turnover, so the image reports metabolism rather than shape.

Dose and cost comparisons that support the judgement. A single plain X-ray delivers a dose in the order of $0.1\,\mathrm{mSv}$, a CAT scan of the wrist in the order of $0.1$ to $1\,\mathrm{mSv}$ depending on the number of slices, and a bone scan about $4$ to $6\,\mathrm{mSv}$, which is why bone scans are avoided in pregnancy and are not used for routine follow-up. Cost runs the other way relative to image content: a plain radiograph is a single fast exposure on inexpensive equipment, a CAT scan needs a rotating X-ray tube, detector array and reconstruction computer, and a bone scan needs a radionuclide, a gamma camera and a waiting period of one to three days. So neither of the two ionising X-ray-based techniques gives the early metabolic information the bone scan gives, and the bone scan gives none of the anatomical detail the other two give.

content.text: Binary star systems.
Read the graph for specific features rather than a general impression: say how many minima there are, how deep each is, and how far apart the minima are.
The spacing between minima is not necessarily the period. In an eclipsing binary the primary and secondary eclipses alternate, so they are separated by half the period.
For the distance, remember that an eclipsing binary's light curve alone gives no distance. The route to a distance is angular (parallax) or photometric (apparent versus absolute magnitude).

items: (a)(i) The graph shows the brightness of the system varying regularly with time. The brightness is highest near days 0, 13, 28 and 42; there is a shallow minimum near day 6, a deep narrow minimum near day 21, and a shallow minimum near day 35. The three minima are separated by 15 days and alternate in depth, which identifies the system as an eclipsing binary: the deep minima are the primary eclipses, when the dimmer companion passes in front, and the shallow minima are the secondary eclipses, half a cycle later, when the brighter companion passes in front. Successive primary eclipses are therefore 30 days apart, so the orbital period is about 30 days. The light curve is also not flat between eclipses, but shows a slow, steady rise and fall over the cycle, which is expected when the stars are tidally distorted and when the eclipse depth depends on the viewing angle.

(a)(ii) The distance cannot be obtained from the light curve: a period of 30 days fixes the size of the system by Kepler's third law but not its distance, so the angular or photometric data given in the original paper are essential and are not retained in this bundle.
