content.text: First-hand investigation into spectra, and the production of stellar absorption spectra.

For the practical, ask what a marker wants to see in a spectra investigation: the same viewing geometry for every source, a way of making the lines sharp, and more than one way of checking the result.
For the spectrum, remember Kirchhoff's three laws as three separate situations: a hot dense source, a hot thin gas, and a cool thin gas in front of a hot dense source.
The dark lines in an absorption spectrum come from the gas, not from the source. Work out which of the two is producing the continuous background and which is removing specific wavelengths from it.

items: (b)(i) Features that increase reliability: the same spectroscope or diffraction grating, the same source-to-grating distance, the same viewing arrangement and the same dark room were used for every source, so the only variable was the source itself; a narrow slit and a collimating lens were used so the lines were sharp and could be compared across sources rather than smeared into a band; each source was viewed several times and the position and colour of the lines recorded rather than relying on a single visual impression; known reference spectra with identifiable lines (such as hydrogen or sodium) were observed through the same instrument to check the scale and confirm the identification; observations were made in more than one order, where the diffraction-grating relation $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ can be checked for consistency; and any observation that did not agree with a repeat or with a reference was recorded and repeated rather than discarded.

(b)(ii) An absorption spectrum is a continuous (rainbow) spectrum crossed by a set of dark lines, so it looks like a rainbow with dark lines running through it. It is produced when light from a hot, dense source passes through a cooler gas that is thin enough to be transparent. The hot dense source emits at all wavelengths and so produces the continuous background. In the cooler gas each atom can absorb only photons whose energy matches exactly the difference between two of its allowed electron energy levels, so a photon of a discrete set of wavelengths is removed from the beam. Because each element has its own unique set of energy levels, each element removes its own unique set of wavelengths, and those wavelengths appear as dark lines. In a star the continuous spectrum is produced by the hot, dense photosphere and the cooler, much thinner outer atmosphere acts as the absorbing gas, so the result is a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines whose positions identify which elements are present in the star's atmosphere. This is why stellar absorption spectra show that the stars are made of the same elements as the Earth, and it is also why the Earth's atmosphere produces dark lines in the spectrum of the Sun viewed from the ground.

content.text: Part (i). A spectra investigation is only a fair test if everything except the source is held constant, so the reliability measures are procedural: fixed geometry, a controlled light path, a dark room to remove stray light, a narrow slit so that each line is resolved, repeated observations, and comparison against reference spectra with known lines. Recording the position of lines rather than describing their appearance removes observer bias, and repeating in more than one order provides an internal consistency check.

Part (ii). The dark lines can only be accounted for by quantised energy levels in the absorbing gas. The energy of a photon is $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, and an atom can absorb a photon only if that energy equals the difference between two of its allowed levels, $\Delta E = hf$, which selects particular wavelengths. Kirchhoff's three laws state the three cases: a hot dense source alone gives a continuous spectrum; a hot thin gas alone gives a bright-line (emission) spectrum; and a cool thin gas in front of a hot dense source gives an absorption spectrum, because the source's continuous light is depleted at the gas's own wavelengths. In the Sun, the photosphere is hot and dense and the outer atmosphere is cool and thin, so stellar spectra are absorption spectra. Since $\Delta E$ values differ from element to element, the pattern of dark lines is a unique fingerprint, which is how the composition of a star, or of the gas between us and a star, is determined from the wavelengths of the lines.

content.text: Astronomers employ a range of instruments and techniques to observe celestial objects. Assess the impact of technological advances on our understanding of the cosmos.

Organise the response by spectral band (optical, radio, infrared, space-based) rather than by a random list, and for each instrument name one specific thing that became knowable only with that instrument.

An impact is a change in what we believe, not a better-looking picture. The marking notes require at least one advance other than optical or adaptive optics, and two or more distinct impacts on understanding.
Close with a value statement about at least one technology, and acknowledge the one real constraint on it, so that the final judgement is supported rather than asserted.

Technological advances have transformed astronomy and, overall, the impact has been strongly positive: they have extended our observation into regions of the spectrum and distances that were previously invisible, revealing the true nature of the universe.

Optical telescopes: the introduction of large mirrors, adaptive/active optics that correct atmospheric distortion, and space-based telescopes such as the Hubble Space Telescope, which observe above the atmosphere, has allowed stars to be resolved and faint objects to be seen, so the size, structure and composition of stars and galaxies can now be studied rather than only their light. Radio telescopes and arrays such as the Very Large Array detect radio waves, revealing cold hydrogen clouds, pulsars, quasars and the cosmic microwave background, so the early universe and the large-scale structure of the cosmos can be mapped. Infrared and space-based telescopes detect the cooler objects — forming stars, dust clouds and distant galaxies — that emit little visible light, and spectroscopy, whether optical or in these other regions, has allowed the chemical composition and velocities of stars and galaxies to be measured. The impact is that our understanding has changed from a static, geocentric cosmos to one in which the universe is expanding and evolving, and that exoplanets and extra-solar planets can be detected and studied. On balance the value of these technologies is very high, although the cost of building and maintaining space-based instruments limits the number that can be launched and some observations must still be made from the ground.

content.text: The Hertsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram depicts a possible life cycle path of a known star. The diagram appears in the published paper only as an 'Awaiting Copyright Clearance' placeholder.

Each labelled point on the path is a stage at which a particular fusion reaction stops or starts. Before reading any point off the diagram, work out what is fusing at each stage and what happens when that fuel runs out.
The class and mass of the star are fixed by where the path stops: a path ending in a white dwarf belongs to a low-mass star, a path continuing to the supergiants to a high-mass one.

For a very massive star, the reason the sequence ends abruptly is not that it runs out of fuel but that the fusion reactions become net energy-consuming. Check the binding energy per nucleon at the end of the sequence.

items: (d)(i) Reactions at each point of the path. On the main sequence, core hydrogen fusion: in the proton-proton chain four protons combine to give one helium-4 nucleus with the release of about $26\,\mathrm{MeV}$, with the CNO cycle as the alternative route in hotter, more massive stars. When core hydrogen is exhausted the star leaves the main sequence and hydrogen now fuses only in a shell around an inert helium core. At the tip of the red giant branch the core is hot and dense enough for helium fusion: three helium-4 nuclei combine to form carbon-12, and some carbon-12 captures further helium-4 nuclei to form oxygen-16. The star then moves to the horizontal branch, where helium fusion continues in the core, and afterwards to the asymptotic giant branch, where helium fuses in a shell around an inert carbon-oxygen core while a hydrogen shell burns above it, adding further material to the envelope. The envelope is then expelled as a planetary nebula and the remnant is a white dwarf. On the white dwarf branch no further fusion occurs: the degenerate core simply cools, and the star moves down and to the right on the diagram as it fades.

(d)(ii) The path followed is the evolutionary track of a low-mass star of approximately one solar mass: main sequence, red giant branch, horizontal branch, asymptotic giant branch, planetary nebula, and finally a white dwarf. Such a star never becomes a supernova and never produces elements heavier than carbon and oxygen by fusion. (d)(iii) A star of more than 10 solar masses does not end as a white dwarf. After core hydrogen and then core helium, its core fuses successively into carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon and finally iron, and at each stage the core contracts and heats further because iron-group fusion releases no energy. When the core can no longer support itself against gravity it collapses in a fraction of a second, and the infalling outer layers rebound and are blown out as a type II supernova. The remnant is a dense neutron star for masses up to roughly 20 solar masses and a black hole above that, surrounded by an expanding supernova remnant containing the heavier elements (iron, gold, lead, uranium) that the star made. The surviving cluster is left behind after the supernova.

content.text: Reading the path. The H-R diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature, so every move on it is a change in one or both of those quantities, and each change is driven by a change in what is happening in the core. Core hydrogen fusion makes the star hot and luminous on the main sequence. When the core hydrogen runs out the core contracts, the envelope expands and cools, and the star moves up and to the right on the red giant branch while fusion continues in a shell. The helium flash ends that phase; core helium fusion then produces a stable helium-burning star on the horizontal branch. When core helium is exhausted the double-shell-burning phase on the asymptotic giant branch begins, and the envelope is finally lost.

Why the mass decides the ending. The path described ends in a white dwarf, which is the fate of a star of up to about 2 solar masses; a path that runs past the supergiant region belongs to a much more massive star. For a star above about 10 solar masses the sequence of fusion reactions continues through carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon to iron, because each of these releases energy while the binding energy per nucleon is still increasing. At iron it stops, since the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve is at nickel-56; beyond iron, fusion absorbs energy, so the core gains no support and collapses.

content.text: The Bohr picture of the atom explains the energy of the photons emitted when an electron falls from an initial orbit $n_i$ to find an orbit of $n_f$. The various energies depend upon the quantity $n_f/n_i$ and the values for this term are given in the table.
Table of values of $n_f/n_i$ for values of $n_i$ and $n_f$ from 1 to 6.

The blanks are all in the region where $n_f$ is greater than or equal to $n_i$. Ask what would have to happen to the electron's energy for those entries to be filled in, and remember that energy must be conserved.

Check the identification of the table entries against the formula $\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_{i}^{2}}\right)$ before using them: for $n_i = 2$, $n_f = 1$ the value should be $1 - \tfrac14 = 0.75$, which matches the printed 0.7500.

The tabulated numbers are dimensionless, so the energy comes from multiplying by the Rydberg energy $hcR = 2.18\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J} = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}$. Convert to joules if the answer is required in joules, and give $E = hc/\lambda$ a final check.

items: (a)(i) The blanks are the entries where $n_f \geq n_i$. Those transitions would need the electron to move to an orbit of equal or higher quantum number, so it would have to gain energy rather than release it. An electron in a stationary orbit emits radiation only when it falls to a lower orbit, because the fall releases the energy difference as a single photon of energy $E = hcR\left(1/n_f^{2} - 1/n_i^{2}\right)$; if $n_f \geq n_i$ the bracket is zero or negative, so no photon is emitted and the transition cannot occur. The table is therefore a triangular list of physically possible emissions.

(a)(ii) Read the bracket for the required fall straight from the table: for $n_i = 4$ to $n_f = 3$ the entry is $0.0486$. Then $E = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV} \times 0.0486 = 0.66\,\mathrm{eV}$, or equivalently $E = hcR \times 0.0486 = 2.18\times10^{-18} \times 0.0486 = 1.06\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. That energy corresponds to $\lambda = \frac{hc}{E} = 1.88\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$, in the infra-red. Any other entry in the table is treated the same way.

content.text: Part (i). The Bohr model puts the energy of an orbit at $E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\,\mathrm{eV}$, so $E_{n_f} - E_{n_i} = 13.6\left(1/n_f^{2} - 1/n_i^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{eV}$. Every blank in the table has $n_f \geq n_i$, which makes this difference zero on the diagonal or negative below it. A negative difference would require energy to be supplied, which an electron in a stationary orbit can only receive by absorbing a photon, and if it absorbed exactly that energy it would be in the higher orbit, not the lower one specified. Because a photon carries a single energy $hf$, no partial absorption is possible either, so the transition is impossible and the entry is left blank. The initial state must be higher, more energetic and further out than the final state.

content.text: You have gathered, processed and analysed information related to the development of atomic theory.
For the source part, treat reliability as a criterion, not a formality: say which sources you used, why they can be trusted, and how you checked them against each other.
For the scientists part, take each in turn and state what the model was before, what observation forced the change, and what the new model got right that the old one could not.
A model that survives because it explains the data is worth more in the argument than a model that is merely elegant. Use each scientist's own experimental result as the reason for the change.

items: (b)(i) Data sources and reliability. Primary sources used were the original papers and the recorded experimental results of the scientists themselves (Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering counts behind gold foil, the deflection angles of alpha particles; Chadwick's account of the bombardment of beryllium with alpha particles), obtained from the original journals, the published lecture notes of the period and museum or university archives that reproduce the primary papers. Secondary sources were used only to interpret them: authoritative textbooks, the Nobel Prize lectures and modern historical reviews. Reliability was achieved in three ways. Accuracy: the primary papers were used in preference to later retellings, and where a secondary source disagreed with a primary paper the primary paper was taken as correct and the discrepancy noted. Relevance: only sources dealing directly with atomic structure at the time in question were selected, and sources about unrelated branches of physics were excluded. Currency and objectivity: the historical record was used rather than later speculation, and where accounts differed the reason for the difference was identified as either genuine scientific disagreement or later reinterpretation, and recorded. Cross-checking was also used: each claim was confirmed against at least two independent sources before being used.

(b)(ii) How the two scientists modified atomic theory. Thomson (1897-1904) produced the first working atomic model. Having shown that cathode rays are streams of particles with mass and charge, he proposed that the atom is a small sphere of positively charged material in which the electrons are embedded, like plums in a pudding; on this model the positive charge is spread out, so an alpha particle should pass through a thin foil with only a small deflection. Rutherford (1911), following Geiger and Marsden's gold-foil experiment, found that about 1 in 8000 alpha particles was deflected through more than $90^{\circ}$ and that some bounced almost back. This could not happen in a diffuse positive sphere, because the electric field inside such a sphere increases steadily with radius but is too weak to reverse a fast, heavy alpha particle. Rutherford therefore concluded that the atom is mostly empty space with all its positive charge and almost all its mass concentrated in a nucleus of radius about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, some 10,000 times smaller than the atom, and he kept the electrons outside it. Bohr (1913) accepted Rutherford's nucleus but showed that this model could not explain why an atom radiates only certain frequencies rather than a continuous spectrum, and why it does not collapse. He imposed Planck's quantum condition on the orbiting electron, allowing only orbits of angular momentum $nh/2\pi$, and treated the energy of each orbit as stationary, so no radiation is emitted between allowed orbits. The photon released on a fall is $hf = \Delta E$, which reproduced the observed line spectra of hydrogen exactly, and his energy levels gave the Rydberg formula. The development is therefore cumulative and evidence-driven: each model was retained where it worked and replaced where it failed, and the experimental result that caused the replacement is the strongest part of the argument.

content.text: Part (i). A secondary-source investigation is judged on the selection of sources and on the criteria applied to them. The four criteria normally assessed are scientific reliability (is the claim supported by data, and is the source peer-reviewed or a primary record), relevance (does it address the question asked), currency (is it up to date for the topic, although for a historical question the period is deliberately restricted), and objectivity (is the author free of bias, and are limitations and disagreements disclosed). The response should name the actual sources and show which criterion decided each selection, not merely assert that the sources were reliable.

Part (ii). The test of each model is whether it accounts for the observations. Thomson's model is rejected because the electric field it allows inside the atom cannot produce the large-angle deflections observed. Rutherford's model survives because a small, dense, highly charged nucleus does produce them, and it correctly predicts that the mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny volume and that alpha particles are scattered most strongly by nuclei. It fails to explain line spectra and atomic collapse. Bohr's model survives because the quantisation of the angular momentum is exactly what suppresses both problems, and because

reproduces the hydrogen spectrum to experimental accuracy. The analysis therefore shows each scientist keeping what the evidence supported and discarding what it did not, which is the pattern the question asks to be identified.

content.text: Australia has a large supply of uranium which may be used in fission reactors to create energy. The equation describes the relevant transmutation reaction:
Analyse how the process described in this equation has been developed into a technology which produces a sustained and controlled amount of energy.
Read the equation for what makes it self-sustaining: count the free neutrons released per fission, then ask what would have to happen for the process to die out.

Distinguish the two components that act on the rate of the chain. One slows the neutrons so that they can be absorbed; the other absorbs neutrons to set the rate. Naming only one of them is the commonest way to lose a mark here.

Do not stop at 'energy is released'. Follow the energy from the mass defect through the fuel to the working fluid and then to the electrical output, and tie the first step back to $E = \Delta m c^{2}$.

The equation shows uranium-235 absorbing a neutron and splitting into barium-141, krypton-92 and three free neutrons, releasing energy from the mass defect. Each of the three neutrons can be captured by another U-235 nucleus, so the reaction is self-sustaining. In a reactor, fuel rods of enriched uranium are placed in a moderator such as water or heavy water which slows the neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed, and control rods of boron or cadmium absorb neutrons to regulate the rate. Coolant water carries the thermal energy to a steam generator which produces steam to drive turbines and generate electricity.

In the equation a slow neutron is absorbed by a uranium-235 nucleus, which becomes unstable and splits into barium-141 and krypton-92, together with three free neutrons and energy. The total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the reactants, and this mass defect is converted into released energy by $E = \Delta m c^{2}$; of the roughly 200 MeV released, about 165 MeV appears as kinetic energy of the fission fragments, which heats the fuel. The three neutrons released are crucial: each can be absorbed by another U-235 nucleus, releasing a further three neutrons, so a chain reaction is possible. Because fast neutrons are less likely to be absorbed by U-235, a moderator such as water, heavy water or graphite is placed between the fuel rods to slow the neutrons to thermal speeds, where the probability of capture is high. Control rods of boron, cadmium or hafnium are inserted into the core to absorb excess neutrons and so regulate and control the rate of the chain reaction; withdrawing them allows it to speed up. Control is also maintained by the use of enriched U-235 fuel and by automatic shutdown systems. In a power station the heat released in the fuel is removed by a coolant that circulates through the core to a steam generator; the steam drives turbines which turn generators to produce electricity, with the condensate returned to the core. Thus the uncontrolled energy release of a fission bomb has been harnessed into a technology that produces a sustained, controlled and safe supply of electrical energy.

content.text: The cyclotron, invented in 1932, accelerates charged particles to a very high speed. The diagram shows the basic design of a cyclotron. The Dees provide a strong magnetic field into the plane of the page.
Split the two Dees' jobs apart. Ask what force keeps the particle on a circular path and therefore what it cannot do to the particle's speed, then ask which part of the machine does change the speed.
The source sits at the centre, so the radius grows as the particle gains energy. Work out what happens to the time for one half-turn as that happens — that is what makes the machine work, or fail.
For part (ii), ask what a high-energy collision buys you that a stationary particle does not: whether the particle and its antiparticle can be created out of the collision energy.

items: (d)(i) The cyclotron works by separating two jobs between the magnet and the electric field. Charged particles from a source at the centre are accelerated across the gap between two hollow electrodes (the Dees) by a potential difference, so an alternating supply is required; the particles then enter a Dee and move in a circular path because the strong magnetic field into the plane of the page exerts a force $F = qvB$ perpendicular to the velocity. That magnetic force can only turn the path round, so it changes the direction of the velocity but never the speed — a magnetic field does no work. The speed is increased only in the gap, where the electric field acts along the velocity. On emerging from a Dee the particle crosses the gap again; the alternating voltage has by then reversed, so it is again accelerated in the direction of motion, its speed rises, and by $r = mv/qB$ its radius grows. Crucially the time for one half-turn, $T/2 = \pi m/qB$, contains no velocity term, so it is the same on every circuit however fast the particle is going; the alternating supply can therefore be driven at a fixed frequency $f = qB/2\pi m$, and every crossing of the gap adds energy in phase. The particle spirals outward, gaining energy in small increments, until it is extracted from the machine. Because the mass appears in the frequency, the machine falls out of step once the speed is high enough for relativistic mass increase to matter, which is why synchrocyclotrons modulate the frequency and why proton synchrotrons use very large magnets.

(d)(ii) Accelerators are how matter is examined at scales no laboratory can reach. Because $E = mc^{2}$, a collision between particles with enough total kinetic energy can create pairs of particles that did not exist before the collision, so new species of matter can be made on demand and identified by the products. In a fixed-target machine much of the incoming energy goes into moving the centre of mass rather than into making particles, so in a collider, where opposite beams meet with the centre of mass at rest, essentially all the available energy is available for creation. Analysing the tracks and energies of the decay products has led to the discovery of the positron, the muon, the kaon, the neutral pion, the W and Z bosons, the gluon and the top quark, and has established the quark model and the Standard Model. Accelerator experiments also probe the internal structure of protons and neutrons and give the evidence for quarks, which cannot be studied inside an atom because the nucleus cannot be examined without destroying it.

(d)(iii) Proton: two up quarks and one down quark, $uud$ (charge $+1$). Neutron: one up quark and two down quarks, $udd$ (charge $0$). Both are baryons, each made of three quarks held together by the strong nuclear force, which acts through gluon exchange and is very strong over short distances and effectively absent beyond about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$.

content.text: Part (i), the two fields. Inside a Dee there is no electric field, but there is a strong magnetic field into the plane of the page. The particle moves with velocity $v$ and experiences $F = qvB$, which is perpendicular to $v$, so it is a centripetal force and the speed is unchanged:

content.latex: qvB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \quad \Rightarrow \quad r = \frac{mv}{qB} \qquad T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB} \qquad f_c = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}

content.text: In the gap between the Dees there is a strong electric field and no magnetic field, so the electric force $qE$ acts along the velocity, changing the kinetic energy by the work done. The period contains neither $v$ nor $E$, only the mass and the charge, so it is constant; the time to cross the gap is much shorter than the time spent inside a Dee, so the driving voltage only needs to reverse twice per turn. Setting the supply frequency to $f_c$ keeps the field in the correct direction at every crossing, and the particle is accelerated repeatedly while spiralling outward as $r \propto v$.
Part (ii). The argument is mass-energy equivalence: the collision energy can become particle rest energy,

content.latex: \gamma m c^{2} \rightarrow \sum m_{i} c^{2} \qquad \text{with } E = \gamma m c^{2}

content.text: so species absent from the starting state appear among the products. In a collider the incoming momenta cancel, so the centre of mass is at rest and the whole collision energy is available; in a fixed target most of the energy is spent on the recoil of the centre of mass, which is why colliders give the greater effective energy for the same machine. The decay products are then used to identify the new particles, which is how the quark model and the Standard Model were established.

Part (iii). Conservation of charge and baryon number fixes the compositions: the proton has charge $+1e$ and the neutron $0$, and each is a baryon made of three quarks, so the proton is $uud$ and the neutron is $udd$.

content.text: Lately, traffic control authorities in NSW have been replacing the incandescent bulbs in traffic lights with arrays of light emitting diodes (LEDs).

Structure first, then operation: name the two doped semiconductor regions, the junction between them, and the direction the voltage is applied. The operation question is then just asking what happens to the electrons at the junction.

The colour of an LED is not a choice made afterwards — it follows from the energy of the photon, which equals the band gap of the compound semiconductor used. That single fact explains why the arrays must be built from separate red, amber and green chips.

For the reasons, look for three distinct categories rather than three versions of the same point: energy and cost, time and maintenance, and the physical properties a signal needs (speed of switching, direction of emission, temperature).

items: (a)(i) Structure: an LED is a p-n junction diode formed from two regions of a semiconductor, one doped with acceptor impurities to give a p-type region and one doped with donor impurities to give an n-type region, joined at the junction. The regions are very thin and small, and the whole chip is mounted in a reflector and covered by a lens to concentrate the light. Operation: a forward bias is applied, with the p-region positive relative to the n-region. This drives electrons from the n-region across the junction into the p-region, where they recombine with holes. In doing so the electrons fall from a higher to a lower energy level in the p-region and the difference is emitted as a single photon, so $E = hf = hc/\lambda = \Delta E_{\text{gap}}$. Because $\Delta E_{\text{gap}}$ is fixed by the compound semiconductor used, each material emits one colour: gallium arsenide with phosphorus gives red and amber, gallium nitride and indium gallium nitride give green, blue and white. Almost all the energy released appears as light rather than heat, and the emission is concentrated towards the junction, which is why a lens is needed to form a beam.

(a)(ii) At least three of the following reasons. (1) Efficiency: an incandescent filament converts only about $5\,\%$ of its electrical energy into visible light, the rest becoming heat, whereas an LED converts the great majority of its input into light, so the same brightness needs far less power and far less money over the life of the installation. (2) Lifetime: an incandescent bulb lasts of the order of 1000 to 5000 hours whereas an LED array lasts tens of thousands of hours, so replacements are rare — which matters at a traffic signal, where the cost of closing a road, hiring a traffic crew and working at height greatly exceeds the cost of the lamp. (3) Temperature: an incandescent bulb runs hot enough to be a fire risk in the housing and degrades; an LED produces very little heat, so there is no ignition hazard and no heat damage to the lens or the surrounding materials. (4) Switching speed: LEDs respond in nanoseconds, whereas the thermal inertia of a filament limits it to about a tenth of a second, so an LED signal can be timed, flashed and sequenced and can display countdowns and priority information that an incandescent signal cannot. (5) Direction and colour: LEDs emit in a narrow cone that a lens can focus sharply, giving a brighter, more clearly defined signal for drivers, and arrays of chips give pure, saturated red, amber and green. (6) Ruggedness: there is no fragile filament or glass envelope, so the signal resists vibration, wind and impact.

content.text: Part (i). Doping the semiconductor deliberately introduces acceptor or donor impurities, producing the p-region and the n-region. Joining them creates the depletion region and the junction barrier. Applying a forward bias lowers the barrier so that the majority carriers cross the junction.

An electron crossing the junction recombines with a hole and its energy falls by the band gap, so the difference is emitted as a photon. Since $\lambda$ is fixed by $\Delta E_{\text{gap}}$ and the band gap is fixed by the material, each compound semiconductor has exactly one emission colour; this is why traffic signal arrays are built from separate red, amber and green chip sets rather than from one adjustable source. The junction is small and the recombination region is thin, so the emission is directional rather than isotropic, and a lens is used to collect it into a beam.

Part (ii). Each reason should be justified quantitatively or practically. Efficiency: the figure of merit for a signal is the light output per watt and per lamp, and on that measure an LED array delivers the same luminance for a small fraction of the running power, which is a direct saving on a 24-hour load repeated at thousands of intersections. Lifetime and the maintenance argument that follows from it: at an intersection the lamp is replaced from a cherry picker on a live road, so the labour and traffic-management cost of a single replacement can exceed the cost of the lamp by orders of magnitude, and a lamp that lasts 30 times longer removes almost all of that cost. Temperature: with a filament at about $2700\,\mathrm{K}$ and roughly $95\,\%$ of the input radiated as heat, the housing becomes a fire hazard in dry conditions and the lens and seals are degraded; an LED runs cool. Switching speed: a filament's temperature cannot change faster than the heat capacity allows, which limits it to roughly a tenth of a second, whereas a junction can switch in nanoseconds — so an LED signal can display a flashing green arrow, a countdown or a tram phase that an incandescent signal physically cannot show. Direction and colour purity: a chip emits into a cone of a few tens of degrees and a lens can collimate it, so the signal is brighter at the driver's eye; and narrow-band red, amber and green are far more saturated and more distinguishable at night, and over distance, than the broadband light of a tungsten filament seen through a coloured filter.

content.text: Computer developments since World War II (1945) have been characterised by increasing performance at decreasing cost. This trend may or may not continue in the future. Assess this statement.
The statement has two halves joined by 'may or may not'. A response that only documents the first half scores in the middle band of the rubric, so give the second half equal space.
Build a dated chain of developments and link each one to performance per unit of cost rather than listing them. The rubric asks for three to four developments, each tied to the trend.

For the future, argue from device physics rather than from opinion: as a dimension shrinks, at what point does tunnelling through the gate oxide and electron leakage into the channel stop producing useful speed, and what does the extra power do to the heat problem?

The statement is justified for the period since 1945 but the trend is unlikely to continue indefinitely. Performance has risen and cost per unit of performance has fallen as a result of the transistor, the integrated circuit, increasing packing density, faster memories and greater storage capacity. However, the trend must slow as devices approach the scale where quantum effects in the silicon become significant, and further gains will come from parallel architectures rather than from faster single chips.

Since 1945 performance per unit of cost has improved enormously. The first computers used thermionic valves, which were large, hot, power hungry, unreliable and expensive. The invention of the transistor in 1947 replaced the valve with a small, cheap, reliable solid-state switch, which reduced size, cost, power consumption and heat. The development of the integrated circuit placed many transistors and their interconnections on a single chip of silicon, and photolithography has allowed the number of components per chip to rise steadily, so the performance per chip has improved while the cost per chip has fallen. Faster clock speeds from improved switching times, greater data rates and larger data storage capacity from improved magnetic and optical media have added further improvements. More recently the use of multicore processors has increased performance without relying on faster individual transistors, and software and networking have made many systems more useful for the same hardware. The trend is not however endless. As the transistor dimensions approach a few nanometres, quantum mechanical tunnelling through the gate oxide and electron leakage become significant, so further scaling produces leakage current and heat rather than useful speed, and the cost of each generation rises steeply. Progress must therefore shift to other approaches — multicore and massively parallel architectures, specialised chips, and eventually quantum computing in which the quantum state of individual devices is used. So the statement is correct for the historical period but should not continue indefinitely, and the physics of the semiconductor device sets a limit that will eventually be reached.

content.text: The resistance of a thermistor as a function of temperature is as shown, and a potential divider sensor and feedback amplifier are then designed.

Write the output voltage as a fraction of the supply before substituting anything, and keep straight which resistor the output is measured across — here the fixed resistor, so the thermistor is in the top arm of the divider.

Sensitivity is a difference divided by a difference: read two points off the graph, find the change in output voltage and the change in temperature. Use a range wide enough that the graph reading is not the dominant uncertainty.
For the amplifier, decide whether the sensor output needs to be buffered or amplified, and choose the configuration that gives the sign and the direction of change you want in the final output.

items: (i) Negative. The resistance-temperature graph falls steadily as the temperature rises, so $dR/dT < 0$: this is an NTC thermistor. The curve is not straight, so the coefficient is not constant - it is most negative at low temperature, where the curve is steepest, and is nearly zero at the top of the range.

(ii) About $+0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ per degree. The output is approximately $3.0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and approximately $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, a change of about $3.0\,\mathrm{V}$ over $14^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so the sensitivity is $3.0/14 \approx 0.21\,\mathrm{V}$ per degree. The sensor can therefore resolve a chamber held at $+20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to within a degree or so.

(iii) An inverting operational amplifier with a gain of about $-1.7$. The sensor output is fed to the inverting input through $R_{i}$, the feedback resistor $R_{f}$ runs from output back to the inverting input, and the non-inverting input is connected to the $0\,\mathrm{V}$ reference of the $\pm 15\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. With $R_{i} = 6.0\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $R_{f} = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, $A_{v} = -R_{f}/R_{i} = -1.67$, so the $+6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ sensor output at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ becomes $-10.0\,\mathrm{V}$, well inside the $\pm 15\,\mathrm{V}$ rails. Any pair with $R_{f}/R_{i} \approx 1.7$ is acceptable, for example $R_{i} = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ with $R_{f} = 16.8\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.

content.text: Part (i), the sign. Read the gradient of the resistance-temperature curve: the resistance falls monotonically from about $11.8\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to about $1.4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and towards zero at $120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so $dR/dT < 0$ and the temperature coefficient is negative. Physically, heating a semiconductor raises the lattice vibration amplitude, freeing more charge carriers, so the conductivity rises and the resistance falls; the fall is not linear because carrier generation and scattering both change with temperature.

Part (ii), the sensitivity of the whole sensor. The output is taken across the fixed resistor, so as the NTC thermistor's resistance falls with rising temperature the output rises - which is exactly the rising curve of the measured output-voltage graph, and the reason the printed divider needs no inversion to give a rising signal.

Sensitivity is a difference of voltages divided by a difference of temperatures, read from the output graph: approximately $3.0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and approximately $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

The reading is a graph reading, so about $0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ per degree is the answer; the value is not constant over the whole range, falling to about $0.1\,\mathrm{V}$ per degree above $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and rising to about $0.3\,\mathrm{V}$ per degree below zero, which is the curvature of the sensor.

Part (iii), the amplifier. The required conversion is $+6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ into $-10.0\,\mathrm{V}$, so the gain must be negative and of magnitude about 1.7. An inverting amplifier gives exactly that sign, and its very high input impedance also stops it loading the potential divider.

Taking $R_{i} = 6.0\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $R_{f} = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ gives $A_{v} = -1.67$ and an output of $-1.67 \times 6.0 = -10.0\,\mathrm{V}$. The output stays within the $\pm 15\,\mathrm{V}$ supply rails for the whole temperature range, since the sensor output never exceeds $12\,\mathrm{V}$. The circuit must be drawn fully labelled: sensor output to the inverting input through $R_{i}$, $R_{f}$ as negative feedback from output to inverting input, non-inverting input to the $0\,\mathrm{V}$ reference, output taken from the op-amp output.

A consistency check on the divider, whose fixed resistor carries no printed value: with $R_{\text{th}} \approx 1.4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the measured output of $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ implies $R = 1.4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, and that value reproduces the printed curve at the other points too ($3.1\,\mathrm{V}$ at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $1.3\,\mathrm{V}$ at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $11.6\,\mathrm{V}$ at $120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), which confirms the readings taken from the graph.

items: 1 mark: part (i) gives the negative sign with justification from the resistance-temperature graph.
2 marks: part (ii) reads the output voltage at $6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and forms the correct ratio for the sensitivity.
4 marks: part (iii) draws a fully labelled inverting op-amp circuit connected to the sensor and calculates a gain of about $-1.7$ with a suitable $R_{f}$ and $R_{i}$.
